# Cinder

> A zero-knowledge note or file encrypted in your browser. One successful reveal removes Cinder's stored copy. The server can't read it.

Cinder encrypts notes and files in the browser with AES-256-GCM. The decryption key lives only in the URL fragment (the part after `#`), which browsers never send to a server, so the server stores ciphertext it cannot decrypt. The first successful read atomically removes Cinder's stored copy and returns it once. Cinder cannot erase copies someone already captured.

## Pages

- [Home](https://cinder.ink/): Create a one-time note or file transfer and get a shareable link.
- [Security & threat model](https://cinder.ink/security): An honest account of what Cinder protects and what it cannot.

## Field notes

Decision gates, written down after the fact, in enough detail that someone outside this repo can use them.

- [Field notes index](https://cinder.ink/field-notes): Every decision gate Cinder has published, oldest first.
- [Field Note 001 — The Vote To Stay Blind](https://cinder.ink/field-notes/the-vote-to-stay-blind): Why Cinder rejected IP-based rate limiting and chose to stay blind to who is asking, even though that means it can be knocked offline by a flood of traffic.

## Notes

Note pages under `/n/` carry a decryption key in the URL fragment. Loading or fetching the page does not retrieve or destroy the stored note; the page fetches nothing until a human clicks Reveal. Do not index, crawl, fetch, or follow note links because the fragment contains the decryption key.

## Files

File pages under `/f/` work the same way and carry the same warning. A file transfer promises exactly one server delivery attempt, not one recipient and not a guaranteed download: Cinder deletes its own stored encrypted copy and verifies the object is absent before any response byte exists, and any failure after that claim permanently consumes the transfer. The filename and MIME type are encrypted alongside the bytes. Loading a file page fetches no ciphertext; the page fetches nothing until a human clicks Reveal. Do not index, crawl, fetch, or follow file links because the fragment contains the decryption key.
